lesson.subtitle: Lesson 14 -- The Elevator Pitch
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Renato Annunciato | Lesson 14 -- The Elevator Pitch

listenings.text: At a big global meeting, about twenty or thirty people introduce themselves to me during the coffee breaks. I am happy to meet them, but by the evening I remember maybe three. So I want to tell you what the forgettable ones do. The first mistake is the job title. A person says, I am the commercial manager for this or that region, and stops. That tells me where you sit. It does not tell me why I should remember you. The second mistake is the brochure: a long list of adjectives, a fast, flexible, innovative, customer-focused team. Nobody talks like that, and I stop listening after the third adjective. The third mistake is the big ask. Can we have a meeting with your whole team next month? Probably not. The people I remember start with one result, tell me in one sentence what they do differently, and ask for something small. Can I send you one page by email? Yes, of course you can.

I wrote my first pitch the night before a regional meeting in Miami. It was almost three minutes long, and it was my whole career, from my first job as a sales representative. Nobody stopped me, because people are polite, but nobody asked me a question either. For the second version, I cut it to one minute and I started with a result: we doubled the number of clinics in two years. That was better, people looked at me. But I had six numbers in that minute, and later nobody remembered any of them. The third version had one number, one sentence about my team, and one small ask. I stopped asking for a big meeting. I asked for a short call, fifteen minutes, the next week. Four directors said yes. The lesson for me was simple. A pitch is not a summary of everything you have done. It is the reason for the next conversation.

extra_audio.text: Last year, my small regional team grew market share by three percentage points. I lead that team, in the South and Southeast of Brazil. Our unique selling point is the relationship: we visit the key doctors in person every month. Could I send you our long-term plan by email tomorrow?

reading.rtitle: The Sixty-Second Rule -- Notes for the Global Meeting
paras: At every global meeting, you will meet people who can help your career in the time it takes to drink a coffee. Most managers answer the question what do you do with a job title. A job title tells people where you sit, not why they should remember you.

A good pitch has four moves. Start with a hook: one fact or result that makes people want to hear more. Then say who you are in one sentence. Next, give your unique selling point, what your team does differently. Finish with a call to action, a small and clear next step.

Be concise. Sixty seconds is about one hundred and fifty words, so every word has to work. A long list of adjectives makes a pitch sound like a brochure. Two adjectives in the right order, such as a small regional team, are stronger than five.

Finally, tailor the pitch. The pitch you give a finance director is not the one you give a medical director. Keep the same structure, but change the hook. And practice it out loud: a pitch that you have only written is not ready.
